passages.t: Weeping at the temple, and a covenant
passages.happening:
‘While Ezra prayed and made this confession, weeping and falling facedown before the house of God’ (verse 1), a very large crowd of Israelites, men, women and children, gathers around him, and they weep bitterly too.

A man named Shecaniah son of Jehiel speaks up. “We have been unfaithful to our God by marrying foreign women from the people of the land, yet in spite of this, there is hope for Israel” (verse 2). “So now let us make a covenant before our God to send away all the foreign wives and their children, according to the counsel of my lord and of those who tremble at the command of our God. Let it be done according to the Law” (verse 3). “Get up, for this matter is your responsibility, and we will support you. Be strong and take action!” (verse 4).

Ezra makes the leading priests, the Levites and all Israel take an oath to do it (verse 5). Then he goes to the chamber of Jehohanan son of Eliashib, and there he eats no food and drinks no water, ‘because he was mourning over the unfaithfulness of the exiles’ (verse 6).

A proclamation goes out through Judah and Jerusalem: all the exiles must gather at Jerusalem. Whoever fails to come within three days ‘would forfeit all his property, according to the counsel of the leaders and elders, and would himself be expelled from the assembly of the exiles’ (verse 8).
passages.hearers:
The book's voice changes here. Chapter 9 was Ezra's own account; chapter 10 speaks of Ezra by name. And the first move comes not from Ezra but from a layman, Shecaniah, and from the people who weep with him.

His speech moves from confession to hope to action. The word for hope, miqveh, is rare. Jeremiah uses it when he calls God himself the hope of Israel. After Ezra's prayer of utter guilt, it is an ordinary man who names hope.

An oath or a covenant was a binding promise made before God, and breaking it invited his judgment. By having the leaders swear, Ezra made the reform a public and shared obligation, not one man's opinion. The penalty for staying away joined two things the community took seriously: losing one's property, which meant losing one's livelihood, and being put out of the assembly, which meant losing one's place among the people of God.

To send away a wife was the language of divorce, which the law allowed and regulated. A divorced wife in the ancient Near East normally went back to her father's household, often taking her dowry with her, and young children often stayed with their mothers. The text says almost nothing about how these women and children were provided for. That silence is one of the most painful things in the chapter.
passages.later:
Jeremiah gives God the name Shecaniah's word recalls: ‘O Hope of Israel, its Savior in times of distress’ (Jeremiah 14:8).

The law that allowed divorce assumed it would happen and put limits on it: a man ‘may write her a certificate of divorce, hand it to her, and send her away from his house’ (Deuteronomy 24:1).
passages.hard:
How should a reader understand a reform that sent away wives and children?

This is one of the most troubling scenes in the Old Testament. Women and children who had done nothing wrong themselves were sent away, and the text says nothing about what became of them. Malachi, probably from the same period, speaks against divorce and against faithlessness to the wife of one's youth (Malachi 2:14-16). And the New Testament tells a believer not to divorce an unbelieving spouse who is willing to stay (1 Corinthians 7:12-14).

Interpreters respond in different ways. Some read the reform as a tragic but necessary measure at a moment when the small community was in real danger of being absorbed into the religions around it, as the northern kingdom had been, so that nothing would be left of the people through whom God's promises were to come. They note that the wives' households were linked to the worship of other gods, that the law of Deuteronomy 7 forbade such marriages, and that the cases were examined one by one rather than settled by a single decree. Others hold that the book records what happened without holding it up as a model for all times, and that later Scripture, in Ruth, Isaiah 56, Malachi and the New Testament, points to a different answer. Some hold both: the reform was a real act of repentance under the old covenant, but it cannot be applied directly to Christians, whose calling in a mixed marriage Paul sets out.

All agree that the passage must never be used to justify shutting people out because of their ancestry, since its concern is faithfulness to God. And nothing in it gives anyone today a warrant to break up a marriage or a family.

A word to anyone who has been hurt by a church's discipline, or shunned by a church or a family. What happened to you may have been wrong, and it is not wrong to grieve it. “The LORD is near to the brokenhearted” (Psalm 34:18). If this still weighs on you, please talk with someone you trust, a pastor, a friend or a counsellor. The Find Help page on this site lists places to turn.
passages.asks: Shecaniah confessed the wrong and still said there was hope. Ask where you need to hear that there is hope in spite of what has been done. And ask who carries the cost when a community sets out to put something right, and whether their cost has been seen.

passages.happening:
‘So within the three days, all the men of Judah and Benjamin assembled in Jerusalem, and on the twentieth day of the ninth month, all the people sat in the square at the house of God, trembling regarding this matter and because of the heavy rain’ (verse 9).

Ezra stands and speaks. “You have been unfaithful by marrying foreign women, adding to the guilt of Israel” (verse 10). “Now, therefore, make a confession to the LORD, the God of your fathers, and do His will. Separate yourselves from the people of the land and from your foreign wives” (verse 11).

The assembly answers with a loud voice, “Truly we must do as you say!” (verse 12). But there are many people, it is the rainy season, and this is not the work of a day or two (verse 13). So they ask that their leaders act for the whole assembly, and that the men of each town come at an appointed time with their own elders and judges (verse 14). ‘Only Jonathan son of Asahel and Jahzeiah son of Tikvah, supported by Meshullam and Shabbethai the Levite, opposed this plan’ (verse 15).

Ezra chooses family heads, each named, to stand for their families. The hearings begin on the first day of the tenth month, and by the first day of the first month the cases of all the men who had married foreign women have been heard (verses 16-17).
passages.hearers:
The twentieth day of the ninth month, Kislev, falls in November or December. On the traditional dating this was 458 BC, about four and a half months after Ezra arrived. It was the season of winter rain in Judah, which explains why the people trembled in the open square, and why they asked for the matter to be handled town by town.

The hearings ran about three months. Each case was heard with the town's own elders and judges, not settled by a single order.

The verb Ezra uses, separate, is badal, the same verb used in 6:21 of outsiders who separated themselves from impurity to seek the LORD. In this book the word always means separating from something, toward God.

On the BSB's reading, verse 15 shows that the decision was not unanimous. Four men are named, and the book records their stand without comment.
passages.later:
Malachi, probably from the same century, speaks against both things this chapter holds together. He condemns marrying ‘the daughter of a foreign god’ (Malachi 2:11), and he gives the LORD's word on divorce: “For I hate divorce” (Malachi 2:16).

Paul, writing to Christians, gives a different instruction for a mixed marriage: ‘If a brother has an unbelieving wife and she is willing to live with him, he must not divorce her’ (1 Corinthians 7:12).
passages.hard:
Did the four men of verse 15 oppose the plan, or oversee it?

The Hebrew of verse 15 can be read two ways. It may say that the four men stood against the plan, or that they stood over it, supervising the work. Most modern translations, the BSB among them, read it as opposition. On that reading, the book honestly records that the decision was not unanimous, and it names the men who disagreed.
passages.asks: The people stood in the rain and trembled, and then they asked for a fair and patient process. Ask how your community handles hard matters: in a rush, or with time, care and a hearing for each case. And ask whose dissent you have heard lately, and whether you listened.

passages.t: The names, and an unfinished ending
passages.happening:
The book ends with a list of the men who had married foreign women. It begins with the priests, and first with the high priest's own family, ‘these descendants of Jeshua son of Jozadak and his brothers’ (verse 18). Four of them ‘pledged to send their wives away, and for their guilt they presented a ram from the flock as a guilt offering’ (verse 19).

Then come other priests, Levites, a singer and gatekeepers (verses 20-24), and the other Israelites, family by family (verses 25-43).

The last verse reads, ‘All these men had married foreign women, and some of them had children by these wives’ (verse 44). Then the book stops.
passages.hearers:
The list names a little over a hundred men, among them seventeen priests, some from the high priest's own family. The leaders had led the way into these marriages (9:2), and the list begins with them.

The guilt offering of a ram followed the law for those who had broken faith in matters holy to the LORD. The same word for unfaithfulness runs through chapters 9 and 10.

There is no celebration at the end of Ezra and no summary, only a list of names. The story of the returned community goes on in Nehemiah, where the same problem appears again a generation later. The reform of Ezra 10 did not settle the matter for good.
passages.later:
The law of the guilt offering speaks of someone who ‘acts unfaithfully and sins unintentionally against any of the LORD’s holy things’ (Leviticus 5:15), and asks for a ram.

A generation later Nehemiah faces the same question: ‘Must we now hear that you too are doing all this terrible evil and acting unfaithfully against our God by marrying foreign women?’ (Nehemiah 13:27).
passages.hard:
What does the last verse say, and how does the book end?

The book's last verse is awkward in Hebrew. The BSB reads, ‘All these men had married foreign women, and some of them had children by these wives’ (verse 44). The Greek book of 1 Esdras, which retells these events, reads instead that the men sent the women away with their children, and English translations vary.

The book ends without saying how the matter ended for each family, and without a word about what became of the women and children. It leaves the reader with names, and with the weight of what it does not say.
passages.asks: The book ends with names and no resolution. Ask what you do with a story in the Bible that does not tie up neatly. And ask how you might pray for families broken apart, in the past and now, without pretending that the cost was small.
